newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks leap on reports tax may be eliminated.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks leap on reports tax may be eliminated.

text.p: Media reports that the government may scrap taxes on securities transactions energised sagging Japanese stocks on Wednesday, driving the key index nearly four percent higher by the end of the day, brokers said.
The 225-share Nikkei average surged 655.72 points, or 3.78 percent, clearing the psychologically important 18,000 threshold to close at 18,013.88. Its March futures jumped 730 points to 18,060.
"In addition to the reports, the market was fuelled by

hopes that more tax reforms, especially of land tax, would follow," said Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities. A revision of the land tax could help financial institutions bogged by property-related bad loans, freeing funds for the real-estate market. It would also enhance Japan's timid economic recovery, analysts said.

"The fact the ruling Liberal Democratic Party voiced the need for a change was also encouraging," a "Big Four" broker said. "The market needed reassurance that the government was serious about the reforms it has been talking about."
Following media reports, a senior LDP official told Reuters that the LDP wanted to abolish the tax as early as 1998.

"Given our policy task of carrying out "Big Bang" financial reforms and putting Japan's securities market on an international footing, we must consider abolishing the securities transaction tax because there are no such tax systems abroad," the official said.
Winners outpaced losers 988 issues to 159 with 103 issues unchanged. Despite the lofty mood of the market, turnover was a modest 360 million shares, little changed from Monday.
The market was initially boosted by strength in Nikkei futures in Chicago overnight where March contracts rocketed over 300 points, brokers said.

"Selling volume started abating on Monday and today, buy-backs of futures by institutional investors and dealers emerged, helped by the upbeat mood," Hisao Suzuki, Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd deputy general manager said. "Foreign investors bought bellwether issues."
Since December, stocks have been at the mercy of the government's plan to raise the national sales tax and end special income tax cuts. Market participants fear the moves
will smother economic recovery.
Most of the ailing bank sector was propped up by buy-backs, with Sakura Bank Ltd up 26 yen at 716 yen. Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd rose 50 yen to 1,870.

However, some regional banks such as Tokuyo City Bank, slipped lower. It shed 16 yen to 118 yen, the largest percentage loser on the first section of the Tokyo bourse. Semiconductor related shares rose due to hopes the sector is headed for recovery. Nikon Corp was up 40 yen at 1,600. Advantest Corp rose 70 yen to 6,200. Tokyo Electron Ltd added 110 yen to 3,980 yen.
Japan Airlines Co Ltd fell three yen to 492 yen on turnover of 4.07 million shares, the fifth most heavily traded issue on the Tokyo bourse first section.
"Airlines have been facing strong selling pressure lately, and with the Nikkei average rebounding, people should be buying the shares back," a trader at a foreign brokerage said.
"The fact that they aren't may be a sign that the rebound is not as strong as it seems," he added.
Brokers said that the Nikkei average's rise was a reaction to its recent plunge and well within technical bounds. The momentum would wane without elements to sustain it, they said.
On a sector basis, there were no major retreaters, but mining, transport equipment, pulp/paper, sea transport and ceramics were the main gainers.
Other indices were also higher, with TOPIX up 29.30 points or 2.17 percent at 1,378.62. The Nikkei 300 rose 5.67 points or 2.22 percent to 261.14.
The second section index was up 4.67 points or 0.27 percent at 1,739.68. Turnover was 6.97 million shares, against 5.88 million on Tuesday.
The over-the-counter index was up 0.50 points or 0.04
percent at 1,240.03.
-- Masako Iijima, Tokyo Equities Desk +81-3-3432-9052 (c) Reuters Limited 1997
